facts.value: 270 m at Main Wharf; over 225 m assessed individually

name: Wellington
location: In Wellington Harbour at the southern tip of New Zealand's North Island, beside the capital's centre.
summary: Run by CentrePort, which is owned by Greater Wellington Regional Council (77%) and Horizons Regional Council (23%). It handles containers, logs, bulk fuel and vehicles, and provides the wharves for the Interislander and Bluebridge ferries across Cook Strait. The 2016 Kaikōura earthquake badly damaged the container terminal, with repairs completed in 2022.
vehicleHandling: RoRo vessels use Aotea Quay, and CentrePort handled 14,706 imported vehicles in the year to 30 June 2026. Containers are handled at the Thorndon container terminal, which moved 145,155 TEU in the same year.
hinterland: Wellington and the lower North Island.

facts.label: Owners
facts.value: Greater Wellington (77%) and Horizons (23%) regional councils

name: Zárate
location: Zárate lies on the Paraná de las Palmas river in Buenos Aires Province, about 60 km north-west of the city of Buenos Aires.
summary: Zárate is Argentina's main river port for finished vehicles, built around Terminal Zárate, a car, container and project cargo terminal run by Grupo Murchison. The town is also an industrial centre with a Toyota factory, so the port handles both new-vehicle exports and imports.
vehicleHandling: Terminal Zárate's vehicle division has 1,530,000 sq m of paved yards and space for up to 61,000 CEU at one time, plus a 230,000 sq m off-port distribution centre. Two pier positions on its 480 m pier can take PCC and PCTC car carriers at the same time, and vehicles are tracked with the terminal's own VLT&T system. The same terminal handles containers, with an annual capacity of 270,000 TEU.
hinterland: It sits on the industrial corridor north of Greater Buenos Aires, next to the Zárate-Brazo Largo bridge across the Paraná, and has barge links to Paraguay and Bolivia.

name: Paranaguá
location: Paranaguá is on Paranaguá Bay in the state of Paraná, southern Brazil.
summary: Paranaguá is Brazil's second-largest port by tonnage and the largest bulk port in Latin America, best known for soya exports. It handled 56 million tonnes in 2021 and has grown quickly as a vehicle port, ranking second in Brazil for vehicle trade in the first five months of 2026.
vehicleHandling: Car carriers work at berth 219, a berth dedicated to RoRo ships, and vehicles are stored at the TCP container terminal and at two specialised vehicle terminals. The port handled 106,725 vehicles in 2025, and in May 2026 it discharged 5,101 electric cars from a single ship, its largest vehicle operation to date. Containers go through TCP, the Paranaguá Container Terminal.
hinterland: Its catchment covers Paraná, Santa Catarina, Rio Grande do Sul, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, parts of São Paulo and Minas Gerais, and Paraguay.

facts.label: Container terminal
facts.value: TCP, Terminal de Contêineres de Paranaguá

name: Rio de Janeiro
location: The port lies in a cove on the western shore of Guanabara Bay, beside central Rio de Janeiro.
summary: Opened in 1910, the Port of Rio de Janeiro is one of Brazil's busiest ports, with a 6.7 km quay front, managed by Companhia Docas do Rio de Janeiro (PortosRio). In 2024 it handled a record 15.4 million tonnes, up 39.7%, and 1.2 million TEU of containers, up 70%.
vehicleHandling: Vehicles go through MultiCar, the port's vehicle terminal, run by the Multiterminais group next to its MultiRio container terminal. MultiCar has what the operator describes as the first multi-storey vehicle garage in a Latin American port terminal, and after an expansion costing nearly R$500 million, which added 560 m of quay, the two terminals share 1,160 m of continuous quay. MultiRio itself has 800 m of quay, 15.3 m of draft and a capacity of 1 million TEU a year.
hinterland: It serves the city and state of Rio de Janeiro, with road links on the BR-040, BR-101 and BR-116 and rail access via MRS Logística.

facts.label: Port authority
facts.value: Companhia Docas do Rio de Janeiro (PortosRio)

name: Santos
location: Santos is on the coast of São Paulo state, about 79 km from the city of São Paulo, with terminals on both the Santos and Guarujá banks of the estuary.
summary: Santos is Brazil's largest port and one of the busiest container ports in Latin America, handling around 147 million tonnes of cargo in 2021. It opened in 1892 and is run by the Santos Port Authority.
vehicleHandling: Most vehicles go through Santos Brasil's TEV vehicle terminal on the left (Guarujá) bank, next to the Tecon Santos container terminal; TEV has an annual capacity of 300,000 vehicles and has handled more than 3 million since 2009. Ecoporto Santos on the right bank also handles vehicles. The port handled 284,100 vehicles in the first half of 2026, of which TEV moved 102,000.
hinterland: It is the main port for the city and state of São Paulo, reached via the Anchieta and Imigrantes highways and by rail.

name: Vitória
location: The port complex lies on Vitória Bay in the state of Espírito Santo, with terminals in Vitória and neighbouring Vila Velha.
summary: Vitória has become Brazil's leading gateway for imported vehicles, accounting for 46% of the country's vehicle trade in the first half of 2026. The port complex has been run since 2022 by the private concessionaire Vports, which handled a record 7.9 million tonnes in 2025.
vehicleHandling: Car carriers mainly use Log-In's Terminal de Vila Velha (TVV), a 108,000 sq m multipurpose terminal with two berths on a 450 m quay, while Comexport operates a dedicated vehicle terminal that it expanded by 16,000 sq m in 2025. The complex discharged 215,000 vehicles in 2025, with a peak of 49,650 in June. In December 2022 TVV also received more than 300 cars shipped in 48 ft containers.
hinterland: It serves Espírito Santo, with road and rail links to south-east Brazil.

name: San Antonio
location: San Antonio is on Chile's central Pacific coast in the Valparaíso Region, the closest major port to Santiago.
summary: San Antonio is Chile's busiest port, handling 23.2 million tonnes and 1.81 million TEU in 2024. It is run by the state-owned Empresa Portuaria San Antonio, with private operators running its container, multipurpose and bulk terminals.
vehicleHandling: Almost all vehicles arriving in Chile come through DP World San Antonio, a multipurpose terminal with a 700 m berth and RoRo facilities, which says it handles over 95% of the country's vehicle imports. In February 2026 it discharged 6,338 vehicles from the Morning Lily, a Chilean record. The port handled 232,107 vehicles in 2024, and containers are also handled by San Antonio Terminal Internacional (STI).
hinterland: It is the main port for Santiago and central Chile.

facts.label: Container terminals
facts.value: STI and DP World San Antonio

name: Cartagena
location: Cartagena is on Colombia's Caribbean coast, with terminals spread around the sheltered Bay of Cartagena.
summary: Cartagena is Colombia's largest port and a major Caribbean transhipment hub. The Puerto de Cartagena group runs the SPRC and Contecar container terminals, and several private terminals operate around the bay.
vehicleHandling: Much of the RoRo traffic goes to Puerto Bahía, on the road to Barú, which has 30 hectares for vehicles, 15,000 standard storage spaces and capacity for more than 140,000 vehicles a year; it handled 38,067 RoRo units in the first quarter of 2026. The Puerto de Cartagena group also handles vehicle imports, exports and transhipment at SPRC and Contecar, with Contecar acting as a hub for RoRo lines.

facts.label: Other terminals
facts.value: SPRC and Contecar (Puerto de Cartagena group)

name: Santa Marta
location: Santa Marta is on Colombia's Caribbean coast in the department of Magdalena, east of Barranquilla.
summary: The Port of Santa Marta is a multipurpose port run by the Sociedad Portuaria Regional de Santa Marta. It is known in Colombia as a RoRo and vehicle transhipment port, linking car carriers from Europe, the Far East and the United States with Panama, Ecuador, Peru and Chile.
vehicleHandling: RoRo cargo is handled by Fast Terminal Santa Marta, a partnership between the port and Fast Terminal International. RoRo traffic rose from 43,000 units in 2018 to 57,000 in 2019, when the port took about 25% of Colombia's vehicle imports. In 2019 it moved 1,274 vehicles from three ships to a fourth in 20 hours, which it reported as Colombia's largest vehicle transhipment.

facts.label: Operator
facts.value: Sociedad Portuaria Regional de Santa Marta

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Vehicle transhipment for the Pacific coast of South America

name: Turbo
location: Turbo is on the Gulf of Urabá in Antioquia, on Colombia's Caribbean coast close to the Panama border.
summary: Puerto Antioquia, near the mouth of the León River at Turbo, began operations on 5 February 2026 after an investment of about US$764 million. It has a 1,340 m quay with five berths and a 16.5 m operating draft for New Panamax ships, linked to a 38-hectare land platform by a 3.8 km viaduct.
vehicleHandling: The terminal is multipurpose, handling containers, dry and liquid bulk and vehicle imports, with part of its quay set aside for RoRo ships. It is operated by PIO S.A.S. under a government concession.
hinterland: It is the closest Caribbean port to Medellín, 312 km by road compared with 637 km to Cartagena, and also serves Colombia's coffee-growing region.

name: Manta
location: Manta is on Ecuador's central Pacific coast in the province of Manabí.
summary: Manta is Ecuador's main port for imported vehicles and a growing transhipment point for car carriers on the Pacific coast. Its international docks are run by Terminal Portuario de Manta (TPM), part of the Chilean group Agunsa, which also handles wheat, soya and other bulk cargo.
vehicleHandling: TPM received more than 67,000 imported vehicles and a record 29,000 transhipment units in 2025, from 146 car carrier calls. Vehicle traffic kept rising in 2026, with 58,839 vehicles discharged in July 2026 compared with 24,980 a year earlier.

name: Guayaquil
location: The port lies on the Estero Salado about 10 km south of central Guayaquil, reached from the Gulf of Guayaquil by an outer and an inner channel totalling about 51 nautical miles.
summary: Guayaquil is Ecuador's main commercial port. The Autoridad Portuaria de Guayaquil acts as a landlord, with private concessionaires running the terminals. Contecon Guayaquil, the container and multipurpose terminal, lost about 62% of its container volume in 2024 when two shipping lines left, then recovered to 502,926 TEU in January to September 2025, up 52.8%.
vehicleHandling: Contecon Guayaquil, operated by ICTSI since 2007 under a concession running to 2046, has 1,625 m of quay and 10 berths, lists roll-on roll-off vehicles among its general cargo, and runs two storage areas for imported vehicles, one bonded. Most car carriers do not come here, though: the Port of Manta handles about 95% of Ecuador's discharges of new cars and roll-on roll-off cargo.
hinterland: It serves Guayaquil, Ecuador's largest city, and inland markets including Quito, Cuenca and Machala.

facts.label: Main car carrier port in Ecuador

name: Dégrad des Cannes
location: Dégrad des Cannes is in Rémire-Montjoly on the Mahury estuary, about 15 km from Cayenne.
summary: Built in 1974 to replace the old port of Cayenne, Dégrad des Cannes is French Guiana's main commercial port and handles more than 90% of the territory's seaborne trade. It is run by the Grand Port Maritime de Guyane, which also manages the Pariacabo site at Kourou. Traffic passed one million tonnes for the first time in 2024 (1,015,303 tonnes, 75,193 TEU, 236 merchant ship calls), then eased to 963,228 tonnes and 74,655 TEU in 2025.
vehicleHandling: The container terminal has three quays: Quay 1 (220 m), Quay 2 (200 m, reopened in 2014, with a roll-on roll-off berth at its end) and Quay 3 (145 m) for smaller ships, and its yard stores both containers and vehicles. Two 51 tonne electric rail-mounted quay cranes were inaugurated on 27 November 2025; before that ships relied on their own gear. Roll-on roll-off cargo, including construction machinery, buses, trucks and cars, came to 12,903 tonnes in 2024, and the tidal access channel limits draft to about 7 m.
hinterland: It serves Cayenne and the rest of French Guiana.

facts.label: Quay cranes
facts.value: Two 51 t electric rail-mounted, in service 2025

name: Georgetown
location: Port Georgetown lies along the Demerara River where it meets the Atlantic, beside Guyana's capital.
summary: Georgetown is Guyana's main port, made up of privately run wharves along the Demerara River ship channel. The Ports and Harbours Division of the Maritime Administration Department (MARAD) provides pilotage, buoyage and channel dredging, and in May 2026 the government signed a US$11.2 million contract with Boskalis to dredge about 9 km of the Demerara channel. The channel averages about 5.5 m at low tide, so the port is served by feeder container ships, car carriers, bulk carriers and tankers rather than large ocean vessels.
vehicleHandling: There is no single vehicle terminal; car carriers and other ships discharge at private river wharves. In May 2026 the Höegh Pacific landed 800 vehicles from Asia at the Guyana National Shipping Corporation wharf, which its agent described as the largest RoRo call to Guyana so far, and customs notices from February 2026 show imported vehicles held at the John Fernandes and GNIC wharves. John Fernandes and Muneshwers commissioned Guyana's first two mobile harbour cranes, 125 tonne units, at their Water Street wharves in February 2025.
hinterland: It serves Georgetown and the rest of Guyana.

facts.label: Vehicle wharves
facts.value: Including GNSC, John Fernandes and GNIC

name: Manzanillo
location: Manzanillo International Terminal is on Manzanillo Bay in Colón, just east of the Atlantic entrance to the Panama Canal.
summary: Opened in 1995 and operated by SSA Marine, Manzanillo International Terminal is one of the main container transhipment terminals on the Caribbean side of the Panama Canal. It has direct access to the Colón Free Trade Zone and a rail link to the Panama Canal Railway.
vehicleHandling: Alongside its container berths, MIT has a 300 m Mediterranean-style RoRo berth. Its RoRo department handles loading, discharge, storage and delivery of cars, heavy equipment and loose cargo, with a target of 60 moves an hour on car carriers.
hinterland: It serves the Colón Free Trade Zone and acts as a distribution hub for Central America and the Caribbean.

name: Callao
location: Callao is on Peru's Pacific coast next to Lima.
summary: Callao is Peru's largest port and its main gateway for vehicles and machinery. It is overseen by the National Port Authority (APN), with APM Terminals running the North Pier and DP World the South Pier container terminal.
vehicleHandling: Vehicles are handled at APM Terminals Callao's North Multipurpose Terminal (Muelle Norte), which takes containers, break bulk, bulk and RoRo cargo and has a 16 m draft. In May 2026 it discharged 5,733 vehicles from the Asian Captain, a Peruvian record for a single call.
hinterland: It serves Lima and most of Peru's import trade.

name: Pisco
fullName: Port of Pisco (Terminal Portuario General San Martín)
location: The port is at Punta Pejerrey on the Paracas peninsula near Pisco, in Peru's Ica region, south of Lima.
summary: Terminal Portuario General San Martín has been run since 2014 by Terminal Portuario Paracas, part of MSC's Terminal Investment Limited. A modernisation costing US$240 million was completed in 2021, and the terminal handled 2.7 million tonnes in 2022.
vehicleHandling: The multipurpose terminal handles containers, break bulk, bulk, project cargo and RoRo vehicles on 700 m of quay, half of it at 14 m depth. Its first car carrier after the modernisation, operated by Wallenius, discharged more than 600 vehicles in 2021, and the operator presents the port as an alternative to congested Callao.
hinterland: It serves the Ica region and southern Peru.

name: Paramaribo
location: The port is on the Suriname River in the Beekhuizen district of Paramaribo, Suriname's capital.
summary: Jules Sedney Harbour, called Nieuwe Haven until 2016, opened in 1965 and is Suriname's main cargo port, covering about 60 hectares. It is run on a landlord model by NV Havenbeheer Suriname, and has won the Caribbean Shipping Association's best container port award several times, most recently in 2022.
vehicleHandling: The Dr. Jules Sedney Terminal has 600 metres of quay and about 18 hectares of terminal, and handles containers (on average about 100,000 TEU a year), break-bulk and rolling stock including vehicles, with regular calls by container, multipurpose and roll-on roll-off ships. The main operator there is DP World Paramaribo, which took over the local Integra Port Services in 2011 and offers roll-on roll-off discharge and wheeled cargo handling alongside a container capacity of 130,000 TEU a year.
hinterland: It serves Paramaribo and the rest of Suriname.

facts.label: Containers
facts.value: About 100,000 TEU a year on average

name: Montevideo
location: The port lies on Montevideo Bay on the Río de la Plata, beside the Ciudad Vieja of Uruguay's capital.
summary: Montevideo is Uruguay's main port and a regional hub on the Río de la Plata, with 19 berths and a maximum draft of 14 m. It is run by the Administración Nacional de Puertos (ANP) and covers about 110 hectares with more than 4,500 m of quays.
vehicleHandling: Car carriers use the ANP's public multipurpose berths, where the port handles exports of vehicles built in Uruguay and transhipment of vehicles made elsewhere in the region to Chile, Peru and Colombia. In August 2023 it loaded 3,500 vehicles onto the Glovis Crystal in three days, and in September 2023 it moved 6,485 vehicles across seven ships. Containers are handled at Terminal Cuenca del Plata (TCP), operated by Katoen Natie.
hinterland: It serves Uruguay and acts as a transhipment point for the wider Río de la Plata region.

name: Luanda
location: In Angola's capital city on Luanda Bay, sheltered from the Atlantic Ocean by the Ilha de Luanda sand spit.
summary: Luanda is Angola's principal seaport and main import and export gateway, handling more than 625,000 TEU of containers in 2023. The port dates back to 1576 and is administered by the state company Porto de Luanda E.P., which licenses the private terminal operators.
vehicleHandling: AD Ports Group, with local partners Unicargas and Multiparques, holds a 20-year concession to turn the Luanda Multipurpose Terminal into a container and ro-ro terminal branded Noatum Ports Luanda Terminal. Groundbreaking took place in September 2025, and the rebuilt terminal is planned to cover 192,000 square metres with a 16-metre draught and to handle more than 40,000 vehicles a year alongside 350,000 TEU of containers. Completion was expected in the first quarter of 2027.
hinterland: The port serves Luanda and inland Angola, with the Luanda Railway running east to Malanje Province and the EN-100 highway giving road access.

facts.label: Ro-ro terminal project
facts.value: Noatum Ports Luanda Terminal (AD Ports Group, 81% stake)

name: Cotonou
location: In Cotonou, Benin's largest city and economic capital, on the Atlantic coast of the Bight of Benin.
summary: Cotonou is Benin's only deep-sea port, opened in 1964, and has been managed under contract by Port of Antwerp-Bruges International since 2018. It handled 9.6 million tonnes in 2024 and 14.7 million tonnes in 2025, with 841 ship calls in 2025. The main container terminal is Benin Terminal, a subsidiary of AGL (Africa Global Logistics, owned by MSC), which is doubling its quays under a €165 million plan announced in 2024.
vehicleHandling: Vehicles are handled by Roro Terminal Bénin, the port's licensed ro-ro terminal operator, and Grimaldi, whose group owns terminal and car park operations at Cotonou, runs frequent ro-ro calls; its Great Cotonou, a 250 metre ro-ro and container ship, first called in May 2025 and the line makes about 100 calls a year. Used vehicles are stored in licensed vehicle parks run by a dozen private operators approved by the port authority.
hinterland: Cotonou is a transit port for Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso, and a long-standing entry point for used cars bound for Nigeria. Nigerian vehicle importers switched heavily to Cotonou in 2016, and more than 10,000 transit vehicles were discharged there in June 2017.

facts.label: Port authority
facts.value: Port Autonome de Cotonou (managed by Port of Antwerp-Bruges International since 2018)

name: Douala
location: On the Wouri River estuary at Douala, Cameroon's largest city, reached from the Gulf of Guinea by an access channel of about 40 to 50 km.
summary: Douala is Cameroon's main port, handling about 95% of the country's port traffic, and is the leading port of the CEMAC region. It has 26 berths along 5.5 km of quays spread across the Douala and Bonabéri banks of the river, and its access channel has to be dredged continuously, with the inner section maintained at about 7.5 metres.
vehicleHandling: Vehicles arrive both by ro-ro and in containers. A description of the port's terminals lists a 100-metre ro-ro berth within the container terminal area at quays 14 to 17, which is now run by the Régie du Terminal à Conteneurs (RTC), a subsidiary of the port authority that took over from the private concessionaire in 2020. RTC is adding 250 metres of quay and 7.9 hectares of yard under a contract awarded to Negri in December 2022, aiming for a capacity of one million TEU.
hinterland: Douala is the principal sea outlet for landlocked Chad and the Central African Republic under preferential CEMAC arrangements.

facts.label: Container terminal operator
facts.value: Régie du Terminal à Conteneurs (RTC), since 2020

facts.label: Channel depth
facts.value: About 7.5 m maintained in the inner channel

name: Pointe-Noire
location: At Pointe-Noire on the Atlantic coast of the Republic of the Congo, the country's only maritime outlet.
summary: Pointe-Noire is the Republic of the Congo's sole seaport and a transhipment hub on the central West African coast. Its container terminal has handled more than one million TEU a year since 2022 and can receive vessels of up to 8,500 TEU.
vehicleHandling: Congo Terminal, a joint venture of Africa Global Logistics (AGL), APM Terminals and Socotrans, has held the exclusive concession for handling both container ships and ro-ro ships at the port since 2009, so cars arriving by ro-ro and in containers pass through the same operator. The concession was extended to the end of 2050, and a new 750-metre East Mole quay with 17 metres of water and 28 hectares of yard is due to be built from 2027.
hinterland: The port gives sea access to the Congo Basin and serves as a transhipment point for the wider central African sub-region.

facts.label: Concession
facts.value: Since 2009, extended to the end of 2050

facts.label: Container throughput
facts.value: More than 1 million TEU a year since 2022

name: Abidjan
location: In Treichville in southern Abidjan, on the Ébrié Lagoon, linked to the Atlantic by the 2.7 km Vridi Canal.
summary: Abidjan is one of the largest ports in West Africa and carries about 75% of Côte d'Ivoire's foreign trade. It handled 46.6 million tonnes and about 1.7 million TEU in 2025, helped by a second container terminal (TC2) with a 16-metre draught that opened in late 2022. The port opened in 1951 once the Vridi Canal allowed deep-sea ships to enter the lagoon.
vehicleHandling: Abidjan has a dedicated ro-ro terminal, Terminal Roulier d'Abidjan (TERRA), which handles ro-ro ships and their cargo on a single site. TERRA handled 39,854 vehicles and 22,617 TEU in 2021 and was awarded Bureau Veritas's Green Terminal label in 2022. Containers go through Abidjan Terminal and the newer TC2, run by Côte d'Ivoire Terminal.
hinterland: The port is a gateway for landlocked Burkina Faso and Mali, which accounted for most of its 3.9 million tonnes of transit traffic in 2025, and also serves Niger.

name: Bata
location: At Bata, the main city of mainland Equatorial Guinea (Río Muni), on the Gulf of Guinea coast.
summary: Bata is the main port of mainland Equatorial Guinea. It was rebuilt and greatly enlarged by Chinese contractors from 2009, and since 1 April 2026 it has been run with Malabo by Alport G.E., a company 51% owned by Türkiye's Albayrak Group and 49% by the state, under a 25-year concession.
vehicleHandling: The sources consulted do not describe a dedicated vehicle terminal, so vehicles are handled at the port's general cargo berths. The expansion by China Road and Bridge Corporation and CCCC First Harbor Engineering added a new terminal with 14.5 metres of water and berths for ships of up to 50,000 tonnes.
hinterland: The government and the new operator aim to use Bata and Malabo as transit ports for Chad and the Central African Republic.

facts.label: Operator
facts.value: Alport G.E. (Albayrak Group 51%, state 49%), from April 2026

facts.label: Expansion contractors
facts.value: China Road and Bridge Corporation, CCCC First Harbor Engineering

name: Malabo
location: At Malabo, Equatorial Guinea's capital, on Santa Isabel Bay on the north coast of Bioko Island in the Gulf of Guinea.
summary: Malabo is the port of Equatorial Guinea's capital, split into an old port and a new port on Santa Isabel Bay, and its main business is serving the oil industry. Since 1 April 2026 it has been run by Alport G.E., a company 51% owned by Türkiye's Albayrak Group and 49% by the state, under a 25-year concession that also covers Bata.
vehicleHandling: The sources consulted describe no dedicated vehicle terminal, so vehicles are handled at the general and container berths. The port has 488 metres of quay at 14.5 metres depth and about 60,000 square metres of container storage, with a further container depot at kilometre 5. Grimaldi's West Africa ro-ro service calls at Malabo.
hinterland: The port serves Malabo and Bioko Island.

facts.label: Operator
facts.value: Alport G.E. (Albayrak Group 51%, state 49%), from April 2026

facts.label: Layout
facts.value: Old port and new port on Santa Isabel Bay

name: Banjul
location: At Banjul, the Gambian capital, near the mouth of the Gambia River on the Atlantic coast.
summary: Banjul is The Gambia's only commercial seaport. It was run directly by the Gambia Ports Authority until 14 February 2025, when Alport Banjul, part of Türkiye's Albayrak Group, took over under a 30-year concession signed on 11 July 2024 that also covers a planned deep-sea port at Sanyang. The port handled 108,012 TEU and 256 ship calls in 2023.
vehicleHandling: Vehicles and machinery are handled over a ro-ro ramp at the northern end of the New Banjul Jetty. The port has two jetties with five berths in all, the two outer container berths (3A and 3B) each 150 metres long with 12 metres alongside. Because space in the port is tight, imported vehicles and ro-ro cargo have also been stored on rented land along Bund Road, and Grimaldi's West Africa ro-ro service calls at Banjul.
hinterland: More than 70% of Banjul's traffic has been transit cargo for Senegal, Mali, Guinea-Bissau and Guinea.

facts.label: Operator
facts.value: Alport Banjul (Albayrak Group), 30-year concession from February 2025

facts.label: Ro-ro
facts.value: Ramp at the northern end of the New Banjul Jetty

name: Takoradi
location: At Takoradi in Ghana's Western Region, about 230 km west of Accra on the Gulf of Guinea.
summary: Takoradi, opened in 1928, is Ghana's older deep-water port and is managed by the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority. It is the country's main port for bulk exports such as bauxite, manganese, timber and cocoa, and also supports the offshore oil and gas industry.
vehicleHandling: Takoradi handles vehicle imports, and its multipurpose berths can take ro-ro ships. The Atlantic Terminal, operated under concession by the Ghanaian company IbisTek, has a 16-metre berth and was procured by the port authority as an integrated terminal for containers, general cargo and ro-ro.
hinterland: Besides western Ghana, the port serves landlocked Sahel countries including Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger.

facts.label: Water depth
facts.value: 16 m at the Atlantic Terminal berth

name: Tema
location: At Tema on Ghana's Gulf of Guinea coast, about 30 km east of Accra.
summary: Tema, commissioned in 1962, is Ghana's largest port and is run by the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA). It handles more than 95% of Ghana's container traffic, 1,668,688 TEU in 2024, most of it at Terminal 3, the deep-water container terminal operated by Meridian Port Services with a 1.4 km quay and four berths.
vehicleHandling: Ro-ro ships use the multipurpose terminal at Terminal 2, which Meridian Port Services handed back to GPHA after moving containers to Terminal 3. It has two berths with more than 11 metres of draught and about 247,000 square metres of paved yard, and GPHA converted it to take general cargo, bagged cargo, ro-ro and bulk vessels. Vehicles shipped in containers are delivered through the Golden Jubilee Terminal, a 97,412 square metre inland clearance depot at the western end of the port with its own car park.
hinterland: Tema serves Accra and the rest of Ghana.

facts.label: Ro-ro berths
facts.value: Terminal 2 multipurpose terminal, two berths over 11 m draught (GPHA)

facts.label: Container terminal
facts.value: Terminal 3, Meridian Port Services (GPHA, APM Terminals and AGL)

facts.label: Vehicles in containers
facts.value: Golden Jubilee Terminal, 97,412 m² with car park

name: Conakry
location: At Conakry, Guinea's capital, on the Kaloum peninsula on the Atlantic coast.
summary: Conakry is Guinea's main commercial port and a landlord port with private operators. Conakry Terminal, a subsidiary of AGL (Africa Global Logistics, part of MSC), holds the concession for the container and vehicle terminal and handled 416,892 TEU in 2025, while the Albayrak Group runs the conventional (general cargo) terminal under a 25-year contract signed in 2018.
vehicleHandling: Vehicles are handled by Conakry Terminal at the container terminal, where a 330 metre berth at 13 metres depth was built for ro-ro and container traffic. The terminal has a 600 metre quay with two berths (10.5 m and 13 m) on a 200,000 square metre platform, and both berths serve as multipurpose berths including ro-ro. Grimaldi's West Africa ro-ro service calls at Conakry.
hinterland: Conakry also targets transit trade for landlocked Mali, with Bamako about 974 km away by road.

facts.label: Ro-ro berth
facts.value: 330 m at 13 m depth, shared with containers

name: Nouakchott
fullName: Autonomous Port of Nouakchott (Port de l'Amitié)
location: On the Atlantic coast about 15 km from central Nouakchott, Mauritania's capital.
summary: The Port Autonome de Nouakchott, known as the Port de l'Amitié (Friendship Port), is Mauritania's main commercial port, built with Chinese finance and opened in 1986. It handled a record 6 million tonnes in 2024, up from 5.44 million tonnes and about 134,000 TEU in 2023, and has about 2,025 metres of quays. A new container and oil terminal, Terminal à Conteneurs de Nouakchott, built under a 30-year concession by Arise and Meridiam, opened in 2022 with a 250,000 TEU capacity.
vehicleHandling: The port has a dedicated ro-ro quay for vehicles and heavy rolling equipment, about 300 metres long with 12 metres of draught, within its multipurpose facilities. Containers go through the Terminal à Conteneurs de Nouakchott, which has a 570 metre quay at 14 metres. Grimaldi's West Africa ro-ro schedule lists Nouakchott calls.
hinterland: Besides Mauritania, the port serves Mali, and transit cargo for Mali and neighbouring countries gets reduced port charges.

facts.label: Container terminal
facts.value: Terminal à Conteneurs de Nouakchott (Arise and Meridiam), opened 2022

name: Casablanca
location: In central Casablanca, Morocco's largest city, on the Atlantic coast beside the Hassan II Mosque.
summary: Casablanca is one of Africa's largest artificial ports, covering 605 hectares and stretching over 8 km, and it is Morocco's leading port for import and export trade. It handles about 21 million tonnes a year, roughly 38% of Morocco's maritime trade, and most of it is operated by Marsa Maroc.
vehicleHandling: Marsa Maroc runs a dedicated ro-ro and car terminal with two ro-ro ramps at 8.2 metres depth and a covered multi-storey vehicle store of 100,000 square metres holding 5,000 units. About 100,000 new vehicles passed through the terminal in 2023. The port also has a container terminal with a 600-metre quay and its own ro-ro ramp.
hinterland: The port serves Casablanca and Morocco's main industrial and consumer region.

facts.label: Vehicle terminal
facts.value: Marsa Maroc car terminal, multi-storey store for 5,000 vehicles

name: Tanger Med
location: On the Strait of Gibraltar about 40 km north-east of Tangier, roughly 15 km across the water from the Spanish coast.
summary: Tanger Med handled 10.24 million TEU in 2024 across its four container terminals operated by companies including APM Terminals and Eurogate. It opened in 2007 and is run by the Tanger Med Port Authority, with an industrial platform of more than 750 companies alongside.
vehicleHandling: The port has two dedicated vehicle terminals with a combined capacity of one million vehicles a year and 20 hectares of storage, 7 hectares of it for common use. They handled 600,872 vehicles in 2024, mostly Renault and Stellantis exports from Moroccan plants, plus 27,410 imports and 34,100 transhipped vehicles.
hinterland: Tanger Med serves northern Morocco and its car and industrial zones, and is a major container transhipment port.

facts.label: Vehicle terminals
facts.value: Two, capacity 1 million vehicles a year

name: Lagos
fullName: Port of Lagos (Apapa and Tin Can Island)
location: On Lagos Harbour in Nigeria's largest city, with the Lagos Port Complex at Apapa and the Tin Can Island Port Complex a short distance to the north-west.
summary: Lagos is Nigeria's main gateway, made up of two port complexes run on a landlord model by the Nigerian Ports Authority. The Lagos Port Complex at Apapa, established in 1913, is the country's busiest and hosts APM Terminals' container terminal, while Tin Can Island, commissioned in 1977, is the second busiest.
vehicleHandling: Vehicles are handled mainly at Tin Can Island, where Ports and Terminal Multiservices Limited (PTML) operates a dedicated ro-ro terminal at berths 1 and 2 for vehicles and containers, built under a build-operate-transfer deal and in use since 2009. Other Tin Can terminals, including Five Star Logistics, handle containers and general cargo, and Apapa handles containers, bulk and break-bulk through APM Terminals, ENL Consortium and others.
hinterland: The ports serve Lagos and south-western Nigeria, with road links north through Ibadan to the rest of the country.

facts.label: Other codes
facts.value: Apapa NGAPP, Tin Can Island NGTIN

name: Dakar
location: At Dakar, Senegal's capital, on the Cap-Vert peninsula at the westernmost point of mainland Africa.
summary: Dakar is one of the largest ports in West Africa, handling around 10 million tonnes a year. DP World has run the container terminal under a 25-year concession since 2007 and is building a new deep-water port at Ndayane, about 50 km to the south.
vehicleHandling: Dakar has a dedicated ro-ro terminal, concessioned to Dakar Terminal for 25 years on 28 November 2014. It covers 8 hectares with 700 metres of quay, and the port authority sees it as a base for vehicle imports to neighbouring countries and for transhipping vehicles from the Americas to other Atlantic African ports.
hinterland: Dakar serves Senegal and neighbouring countries, including Mali and The Gambia.

facts.label: Ro-ro terminal
facts.value: Dakar Terminal, 8 ha, 700 m of quay (concession from 2014)

name: Freetown
fullName: Port of Freetown (Queen Elizabeth II Quay)
location: At Cline Town in Freetown, Sierra Leone's capital, on the Sierra Leone River estuary.
summary: Freetown's commercial port is the Queen Elizabeth II Quay, a landlord port under the Sierra Leone Ports and Harbours Authority (SLPHA). Freetown Terminal Limited, a subsidiary of AGL (Africa Global Logistics, part of MSC) in which the government holds 20%, has run the container terminal since 2011, and Nectar Sierra Leone Bulk Terminal runs berths 1 and 2 for bulk and break bulk. A new 270 metre quay opened in 2018 lets the port take ships of about 6,000 TEU.
vehicleHandling: Since 2011 the government has concessioned both container and vehicle operations to Freetown Terminal, which manages berths 3 to 6 at the Queen Elizabeth II Quay, including the container yard and ro-ro cargo. There is no separate car terminal. Freetown Terminal lists 15 ro-ro tractor units among its equipment, and Grimaldi's West Africa ro-ro service calls at Freetown.
hinterland: The port handles Sierra Leone's main imports and exports.

facts.label: Port authority
facts.value: Sierra Leone Ports and Harbours Authority

facts.label: Ro-ro berths
facts.value: Berths 3 to 6, Queen Elizabeth II Quay

facts.label: Bulk terminal
facts.value: Nectar Sierra Leone Bulk Terminal, berths 1 and 2

name: Lomé
location: At Lomé, Togo's capital, on the Gulf of Guinea coast close to the border with Ghana.
summary: Lomé, opened in 1968, has 16.6 metres of water, the deepest on the West African coast, and is sheltered by two breakwaters. It handled about 22 million tonnes including 1.2 million containers in 2018 and carries over 80% of Togo's trade. The Lomé Container Terminal (LCT) has a 1,050-metre quay with 16.6 metres of water.
vehicleHandling: The port authority lists 600,000 square metres of parking for used vehicles, including a dedicated 13,000 square metre facility, and a 40,000 square metre Sahel Terminal for vehicles bound for Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. General cargo is worked at Mole 1, a pier with four berths.
hinterland: Lomé serves landlocked Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, as well as trade with eastern Ghana.

name: Apra Harbor
fullName: Jose D. Leon Guerrero Commercial Port (Port of Guam)
aliases: Jose D. Leon Guerrero Commercial Port
location: On Cabras Island in Piti, in the inner reaches of Apra Harbor on the west coast of Guam.
summary: Guam's only commercial deepwater port, run by the Port Authority of Guam, an autonomous public corporation set up in 1975, and renamed in 2002 after its first commercial port manager. It handles over 90 per cent of the island's imports, and in FY2020 handled 85,143 TEU and 1,112,106 tonnes of cargo. It also serves ships trading to the Northern Marianas and the Micronesian islands.
vehicleHandling: The sources describe no dedicated RoRo terminal: cars are handled across the port's 2,650 ft of docking space for container, break-bulk, fishing and passenger vessels and its 26.5 acre container yard. Equipment includes two rail-mounted gantry cranes of 40 short tons, two rubber-tyred gantry cranes and a 104 tonne mobile harbour crane. Matson, the main carrier of cars from the US West Coast, says it ships hundreds of cars a month to and from Guam.
hinterland: The whole island of Guam. Cargo for Saipan and the Federated States of Micronesia is also transhipped here onto connecting ships.

name: Saipan
location: On Tanapag Harbor on the west side of Saipan, the main island of the Northern Mariana Islands.
summary: The largest port in the Northern Mariana Islands, managed by the Commonwealth Ports Authority. It has 2,600 ft of berthing space and a 22 acre container yard, and its channel and berths have been deepened to a uniform 40 ft for medium and deep draught ships. Carriers listed as serving it include Matson, Swire Shipping, PIL and Kyowa Shipping.
vehicleHandling: No dedicated RoRo facility is described, so vehicles are worked across the general commercial dock with containers. Terminal and stevedoring work is done by Saipan Stevedore Company, founded in 1964, whose equipment includes forklifts of up to 40 tonnes, a 50 tonne crane, and tractors and chassis for hauling containers.

name: Pohnpei
location: On Dekehtik, also called Takatik Island, near Kolonia on Pohnpei, the state that holds the national capital, Palikir.
summary: Pohnpei's only commercial seaport, owned and operated by the Pohnpei Port Authority. In 2016 it handled around 2,000 inbound TEU, 70,000 tonnes of breakbulk and 25,000 tonnes of fuel, with little outbound traffic. The main wharf serves international cargo ships, tankers and purse seiners, with a domestic wharf alongside and the separate Takatik Fishing Wharf to the south.
vehicleHandling: No dedicated RoRo berth is described: vehicles cross the main international cargo wharf with containers and breakbulk. The port authority leases cargo handling to a private operator, which works with top loaders and forklifts, and a 7,500 m2 outside storage area is used for general cargo and vehicles.
hinterland: Pohnpei island and the outer islands of Pohnpei State, which are reached by domestic ships from the adjacent wharf.

name: Chuuk
location: On Weno, formerly Moen, Island inside Chuuk Lagoon.
summary: Chuuk's international port and the hub for domestic shipping to islands inside and outside the lagoon. In 2014, 72 ships called and container throughput was 1,155 TEU, and in 2019 the World Bank put current traffic at about 700 full import and 700 empty export containers a year. The port is overseen by the Chuuk State Department of Transportation, Communication and Infrastructure.
vehicleHandling: Vehicles arrive with container freight across two general docks of about 190 m and 185 m; no RoRo facility is described. There are no shore container cranes, so ships discharge with their own gear, at 6 to 10 containers an hour. Terminal services and stevedoring are contracted to the private company Transco.
hinterland: Weno and the other islands of Chuuk Lagoon and the outer islands, served by small domestic cargo and passenger boats from the port.

facts.label: Port oversight
facts.value: Chuuk State Department of Transportation, Communication and Infrastructure

name: Yap
location: In Tomil Harbour at Colonia, the capital of Yap State, on Yap Island.
summary: Tomil Port serves international cargo ships, fuel tankers and the occasional longliner. In 2019 it was served by three multi-purpose shipping lines about every two weeks, with 15 to 30 full inbound TEU per call. The harbour is 5 to 15 m deep and the entrance channel 7 to 10 m.
vehicleHandling: A 264 m main dock handles international cargo, and a concrete RoRo berth at the eastern end of the port takes ramp vessels. There are no container cranes, so ships use their own gear, and terminal services are provided by a private operator under the Yap State Department of Public Works and Transportation. Container freight and vehicles are the port's main imports.
hinterland: Yap's main islands and the state's outer islands, which are reached from the two domestic docks.

facts.label: Port oversight
facts.value: Yap State Department of Public Works and Transportation

facts.label: RoRo berth
facts.value: Concrete ramp berth at the eastern end

name: Kosrae
location: At Okat on Kosrae, the easternmost state of the federation and a single island with no outer islands.
summary: Kosrae's primary commercial port, handling all commercial shipping and fishing. In 2019 it received two to three international multipurpose vessel calls a month, 25 to 30 a year, and handled 600 to 700 TEU a year including empties. Fishing vessels have to stop unloading and leave the berth when a cargo ship arrives.
vehicleHandling: Cargo, including any vehicles, crosses a single main dock of about 170 m shared with the fishing fleet; no RoRo berth is described. The Kosrae Port Authority maintains the infrastructure and leases terminal and stevedoring work to a private company, Kosrae Terminal Services and Stevedoring Company.
hinterland: The island of Kosrae.

name: Majuro
location: Delap Dock lies on the southern lagoon shore of Majuro Atoll, about 1 km from Majuro town, and is reached through the Calalin Channel on the atoll's north side.
summary: Delap Dock is the main international cargo port of the Marshall Islands, run by the Republic of the Marshall Islands Ports Authority. It handled 78 vessel calls and 1,129 TEU in 2019, with regular sailings from Japan, Korea and Fiji. Carriers listed as serving it include Matson, Swire Shipping, Neptune Pacific Direct Line and PIL.
vehicleHandling: There is no RoRo berth: Delap is a general cargo wharf 308 m long, and vehicles are listed among the general containers, reefers and breakbulk that cross it. There are no shore cranes, so geared ships discharge with their own cranes, and the stevedore and terminal operator, Majuro Stevedore and Terminal Company (MSTCO), moves boxes with a reach stacker and forklifts. Containers are delivered to consignees on MSTCO chassis.
hinterland: MSTCO delivers containers by prime mover and chassis to consignees across Majuro Atoll, where they are usually left on the trailer for up to 10 days. Outer islands are served by domestic ships from Uliga Dock, also in Majuro.

name: Ebeye
location: Ebeye port sits on the lagoon shore of Ebeye Island in the south of Kwajalein Atoll, 5.5 km from the US military port on Kwajalein Island and 442 km from Majuro.
summary: Ebeye is the Marshall Islands' second international port, handling about 700 TEU and two scheduled freight calls a month in 2022. International ships arrive en route from Majuro and Guam, and the dock also serves domestic vessels and the ferry from Kwajalein.
vehicleHandling: The main dock is a basic open wharf of 120 m with no cranes or reach stacker, so ships discharge containers with their own gear and they are left at the dock edge; stevedoring is by Kwajalein Atoll Stevedoring Company (KASCO). A separate RoRo landing about 550 m north of the dock, around 35 m wide, takes landing craft and RoRo vessels, mainly for heavy equipment.
hinterland: Ebeye is a small island with no covered port storage, so goods stay in containers on the dock until consignees collect them.

name: Betio
location: Betio port lies on Betio islet at the western end of South Tarawa, inside Tarawa Atoll's reef, about 6 km from the capital's centre.
summary: Betio is the main port of entry for Kiribati imports and the transhipment point for domestic ships to the outer islands. It is managed by the Kiribati Ports Authority, and international lines calling include Kyowa Shipping, Swire Shipping and Neptune Pacific Direct Line, generally about two international vessels twice a month.
vehicleHandling: There is no RoRo berth: all international cargo uses a single conventional berth of 200 m with 8.5 m draft, and ships discharge containers with their own cranes. The Kiribati Ports Authority carries out stevedoring and moves boxes with a 50 t mobile crane, a 40 t reach stacker and forklifts, so vehicles arrive by container or as general cargo over that berth.
hinterland: Betio is linked by road to Bairiki and the rest of South Tarawa, a linear urban strip about 30 km long; outer islands are reached by domestic vessels.

facts.value: About 600 x 20 ft and 400 x 40 ft

facts.value: Shipping Agency of Kiribati (Swire, Kyowa); One Stop Shipping Agency (NPDL)

name: Lae
location: At the head of the Huon Gulf near the mouth of the Markham River on the north coast of mainland Papua New Guinea, in Morobe Province.
summary: Lae is Papua New Guinea's largest and busiest port, handling about half of the country's trade (2026). Its international container operations have been run since early 2018 by ICTSI's South Pacific International Container Terminal (SPICT) at the Lae Tidal Basin, under a 25-year concession granted by PNG Ports Corporation in 2017. Swire Shipping's North Asia Express has called weekly from Hong Kong since August 2025.
vehicleHandling: Cars from outside the region arrive in containers through SPICT's terminal at the Lae Tidal Basin, which is worked with mobile harbour cranes and hybrid rubber-tyred gantries (three delivered in 2019). No dedicated RoRo car terminal or regular RoRo car service to Lae was found.
hinterland: Lae sits at the start of the Highlands Highway, PNG's main road corridor to the Highlands, and its hinterland of Morobe and five Highlands provinces holds about half the country's population.

facts.label: Terminal operator
facts.value: ICTSI South Pacific International Container Terminal (SPICT)

facts.label: Weekly direct service
facts.value: Swire North Asia Express from Hong Kong (since August 2025)

name: Port Moresby
location: On Motukea Island, about 12 km from the centre of Port Moresby, the capital, on the south coast of mainland Papua New Guinea.
summary: Motukea International Terminal (MIT) is the only facility in Port Moresby that handles international containers and is operated by ICTSI under a 25-year concession signed with PNG Ports Corporation in 2017. The terminal stands on land reclaimed with about 1.3 million cubic metres of dredged coral rock, clay and sand. Swire Shipping's fortnightly service from Brisbane reaches it in about 5 days (2024).
vehicleHandling: ICTSI states that MIT handles international containers as well as RoRo and breakbulk vessels, using shore-based mobile cranes, for ships with drafts under 12.5 m. Cars from outside the region normally arrive in containers; the terminal recorded 31 container moves per hour in September 2026 and was preparing to add rubber-tyred gantries.
hinterland: Port Moresby and the National Capital District.

name: Honiara
location: On the Point Cruz peninsula in central Honiara, the capital, on the north coast of Guadalcanal.
summary: The Port of Honiara is the main port of entry for Solomon Islands and is managed by the Solomon Islands Ports Authority (SIPA), which also carries out all stevedoring. A second international wharf and container yard, built with a Japanese (JICA) grant, was commissioned in 2016. The port handled 294 international vessel calls and 33,830 TEU in 2023.
vehicleHandling: There are two international berths: Berth 1 (110 to 130 m) and Berth 2 (150 m, up to about 12 m draft), which is Ro-Ro capable. There are no shore cranes, so containers are landed with ships' gear and handled by SIPA's reach stackers and forklifts; cars from outside the region normally arrive in containers.
hinterland: Cargo leaves by road across Guadalcanal or is reshipped to the outer islands by ferry and small boat from the adjacent Domestic Wharf.

name: Port Vila
fullName: Port of Port Vila (Lapetasi International Wharf)
location: In Port Vila harbour on Efate Island, Shefa Province, the site of Vanuatu's capital.
summary: Port Vila is Vanuatu's principal port. International cargo ships use the Lapetasi International Wharf, a 200 m container berth financed by a Japanese government loan and opened in February 2018, while the older Main International Wharf takes cruise ships and tankers. The Main Wharf was damaged in the earthquake of 17 December 2024 and was still unrepaired in February 2025, but Lapetasi remained in operation.
vehicleHandling: Lapetasi is a container berth with 13 m alongside and no shore cranes. Ifira Port Development Services (IPDS) handles all stevedoring and works the yard with 45-tonne reach stackers; no RoRo equipment is listed, so cars arrive in containers.
hinterland: Efate Island and the capital; cargo for other islands is reshipped on domestic vessels.

facts.label: Cargo berth
facts.value: Lapetasi International Wharf, 200 m, 13 m alongside

name: Luganville
fullName: Port of Luganville International Wharf, Espiritu Santo
location: On the south-east coast of Espiritu Santo in Sanma Province, northern Vanuatu, about 2 km from Luganville town.
summary: Luganville is Vanuatu's second international port. Its main wharf was rehabilitated and extended to a 361 m berth with a Chinese Eximbank concessional loan, with work running from July 2015 to August 2017. It handled 31 vessel calls and 5,024 TEU in 2022.
vehicleHandling: The single 360 m international berth, with about 12 m at the wharf front, is shared by cargo and cruise ships and has no cranes, so ships must use their own gear (minimum 38 t). Northern Islands Stevedoring Company (NISCOL) handles all stevedoring with large forklifts and sidelifters; cars arrive in containers, and the container freight station holds about 1,000 TEU.
hinterland: Espiritu Santo and the northern islands, with the adjacent Samansen Wharf serving domestic ships and ferries.

facts.label: International berth
facts.value: 360 m, about 12 m at the wharf front

facts.label: Feeder
facts.value: Neptune Pacific AUSPAC, alternate sailings from Brisbane (2026)

name: Tibar Bay
location: At Tibar Bay in Liquica municipality, about 12 km west of Dili on the north coast of Timor.
summary: Tibar Bay Port began operating on 30 September 2022 and took over all container ship operations from the old Port of Dili, which now serves domestic ferries and cruise ships. It is run by Timor Port, a public-private partnership under a 30-year concession signed in 2016 with the Bolloré group, and is the only port in the country able to receive international cargo vessels. It handled 58,267 TEU between October 2022 and July 2023, almost all of it imports.
vehicleHandling: Tibar has 630 m of quay in two berths with 16 m draft, one for container ships and one for general cargo, worked by ship-to-shore gantries, rubber-tyred gantries and reach stackers. Cars from outside the region arrive in containers at Tibar; RoRo loading continues at the old Dili port, but only for domestic ferries to Oecusse and Atauro.
hinterland: A paved road links the port to Dili; beyond the capital, cargo moves with small trucking firms on more constrained roads.

facts.label: Feeder
facts.value: Swire East Timor Service from Singapore via Surabaya, every 10 days (2024)

name: Apia
location: Apia's international port lies at Matautu on the harbour of Samoa's capital, on the north coast of Upolu.
summary: Apia is Samoa's international cargo port and is run by the Samoa Ports Authority. It is called weekly by Neptune Pacific's NZPAC service from Auckland and Tauranga, and also by Matson's South Pacific services (2026).
vehicleHandling: The port has two main wharves, No. 1 at 165 metres with 9.5 metres alongside and No. 2 at 185 metres with 10.4 metres alongside, backed by a 1.8 hectare container park. The sources describe no dedicated RoRo ramp; cars arrive on container services and are handled through the container berths.
hinterland: Apia is Samoa's capital and main town, on Upolu.

name: Pago Pago
location: Pago Pago lies in a deep, sheltered natural harbour on Tutuila, the main island of American Samoa.
summary: Pago Pago is American Samoa's main port, managed by the territory's Port Administration, with a container terminal, a multi-use wharf for cruise ships and an inter-island terminal. It is called by Neptune Pacific's NZPAC service from New Zealand and by Matson from both Auckland and, via Honolulu, the US West Coast.
vehicleHandling: Containers are handled at the port's container terminal, worked by two stevedoring companies, Harbor Maritime and Stevedores and Peter E. Reid Stevedore. The sources describe no dedicated RoRo berth, and the lines calling are container services, so cars come through the container terminal.
hinterland: Tutuila is the main populated island; the Manu'a group is served through small local harbours at Ofu, Ta'u and Faleasao.

facts.label: Stevedores
facts.value: Harbor Maritime and Stevedores; Peter E. Reid Stevedore

name: Nuku'alofa
location: Queen Salote International Wharf is in Nuku'alofa, Tonga's capital, on the north coast of Tongatapu.
summary: Queen Salote International Wharf is Tonga's only deep-sea port and handles about 98 per cent of the country's imports, run by Ports Authority Tonga. A major rebuild of Wharf 1 and a 45 metre extension of Wharf 2, funded by the Asian Development Bank and Australia, was due to finish in 2026 and is expected to lift capacity from 30,000 to 45,000 TEU a year (2024).
vehicleHandling: Queen Salote Berths 1 and 2 are multi-purpose and can take RoRo vessels up to 110 metres with 11 metre drafts. The container terminal can store up to 700 containers, with 63 reefer plugs.
hinterland: Tongatapu is the main island; the Vava'u and Ha'apai groups are reached by inter-island shipping, and some Matson voyages call Vava'u directly.

facts.label: Multi-purpose berths
facts.value: Queen Salote Berths 1 and 2, RoRo vessels up to 110 m

name: Avatiu
location: Avatiu harbour is on the north coast of Rarotonga, next to the capital Avarua.
summary: Avatiu is the Cook Islands' primary international port, run by the Crown-owned Ports Authority, and handles about 90 per cent of food imports and all of the country's fuel. An Asian Development Bank project in 2011 and 2012 widened the entrance, deepened the berth and rebuilt the quay.
vehicleHandling: Since the rebuild, container ships and tankers up to 120 metres long can berth alongside the quay. The sources describe no dedicated RoRo ramp; the lines calling from Auckland are container services, so cars come across the container quay.
hinterland: Some Auckland sailings continue from Rarotonga to Aitutaki.

name: Funafuti
location: Funafuti port is towards the northern end of Fongafale islet, on the sheltered lagoon side of Funafuti atoll.
summary: Funafuti is Tuvalu's only international port, with an international cargo wharf and a domestic wharf for the inter-island ships. It is served via Fiji by Neptune Pacific's Capitaine Wallis rotation and by Swire Shipping connections through Suva (2026).
vehicleHandling: The international cargo wharf is 80 metres long and the domestic wharf 50 metres, with a port operations area of about 9,000 square metres, of which 6,000 is container storage (2022). There is no RoRo facility in the sources; cars arrive on small container ships and are handled over the international cargo wharf.
hinterland: The outer atolls are served by government inter-island ships berthing at the domestic wharf.

name: Mata-Utu
location: Mata-Utu's commercial port is on the east coast of Wallis (Uvea), inside the lagoon, next to the territory's capital.
summary: Mata-Utu is the commercial port through which Wallis and Futuna is supplied, managed by the territory's maritime affairs and ports service. An extension finished at the end of 2013 added an 8,000 square metre platform and a new 60 metre quay, and Wallis handled 1,482 containers in 2017.
vehicleHandling: Containers are landed at the commercial quay and handled by one of two private stevedoring firms using mobile equipment. The sources describe no RoRo service, so cars arrive in containers on the Fiji rotation.
hinterland: Some containers are unpacked at Wallis and repacked for Futuna, which has its own small port at Leava.
